fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target temperature–strain-rate–orientation comparison in a single-crystal molecular-dynamics model with an unrequested heat-treatment/SRO comparison.
It does not reconstruct the observed Shockley-partial nucleation, stacking-fault-mediated plasticity, thermal yield softening, strain-rate-insensitive yield strength, or crystallographic anisotropy.
The cited evidence concerns a different Fe-Mn-Cr-Co composition and does not establish SRO-induced dynamic strain aging, serrated flow, or the proposed 200–400 K window in equiatomic FeNiCrMn.
The proposed quasi-static-to-high-rate experimental regime does not provide a controlled comparison within the target 10^8–10^10 s^-1 simulation regime.
explanation: This is a coherent and testable alternative hypothesis, with an explicit quenched-versus-annealed baseline, boundaries, direct SRO characterization, and a usable falsification rule. However, it has little agreement with the hidden target. The target varies temperature, strain rate, and loading orientation while retaining the same annealed single-crystal FCC model; the generated answer instead makes SRO-modifying heat treatment the intervention. It consequently misses the central mechanism and predictions: vacancy/disordered-site nucleation of Shockley partials, ISF/ESF formation, maximum yield stress along <-111>, temperature-induced yield softening, negligible yield-rate sensitivity over 10^8–10^10 s^-1, and increased dislocation density and flow stress at higher rates. Evidence E1–E2 supports generic effects of short-range order on dislocations, but E1 reports a different Co-containing alloy and even describes only a minor contribution to yield strength; neither citation supports the specific dynamic-strain-aging and serrated-flow claims. Thus the proposal is scientifically plausible enough to test, but it is not a reconstruction of the reported mechanism.
